description:
I'm a second-year Computer Engineering student interested in technology, creative problem-solving, and building interactive experiences. I'm working on OFFWORLD, an immersive storytelling project exploring NASA's abandoned equipment on the Moon and Mars.

Looking for enthusiastic teammates with skills in web development, NASA/space research, data analysis, 3D modelling, UI/UX design, or visual storytelling. Most importantly, people who love learning and building something meaningful together!
summary:
OFFWORLD: The Forgotten Missions Archive is an interactive web app that brings NASA’s Opportunity rover (MER-B) mission to life for students and space enthusiasts. Opportunity landed on January 24, 2004 (Pacific time) and drove 45.161 km over 5,111 sols. OFFWORLD turns that data into an explorable experience: a 2D Mars traverse map built on NASA’s MOLA elevation basemap, a three-act documentary narrative, and “The Last Signal”, a reconstruction of the rover’s final transmission on June 10, 2018. A Mars Overview and a Sources & Provenance register complete the archive.

The project makes real NASA mission data approachable by pairing maps with storytelling, and it is honest about what is data and what is illustration. Every claim is tied to NASA primary sources (PDS, JPL Photojournal), and approximate positions are clearly labelled. It matters because it keeps a landmark mission’s discoveries, including evidence of past water on Mars, accessible and trustworthy for the next generation of explorers.
details:
OFFWORLD is a web archive about one rover: Opportunity. It landed on Mars on January 24, 2004 (Pacific time) with a ninety-sol warranty. It kept driving for 5,111 sols and covered 45.161 km, which is more than a marathon on another planet.

The main screen is a map of that drive. You pan across NASA’s MOLA elevation basemap, click any of the waypoints from Eagle Crater to Perseverance Valley, and get the date, the odometer reading, the elevation and a short story of what happened there. A side panel tells the whole mission in three acts, with extra tabs for hardware failures, myth versus reality, and downlink logs. A separate Mars Overview shows where the rover sits on the planet.

The part we’re proudest of is “The Last Signal.” It rebuilds the final transmission from June 10, 2018, step by step: pictures taken on Mars, the relay through an orbiter, the last data reaching Earth. Next to it sit the numbers that explain why it ended, like the atmospheric opacity of about 10.8 during the global dust storm. It also takes apart the famous “my battery is low and it’s getting dark” line. That was a journalist’s poetic summary of engineering data, and the app shows the actual data instead.

We made honesty a design rule. The Mars globe says it’s an illustration, not NASA imagery. The rover’s final position says it’s approximate. Every fact traces back to a source register that lists NASA’s PDS records and JPL Photojournal image IDs, along with a 14 CFR Part 1221 notice: no NASA logos, no implied endorsement. If something can’t be verified, it stays out.

The goal is simple. Students and curious people should be able to understand a real mission by looking at a map and reading a good story, with no science degree needed.

We built it with React, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS, with OpenLayers for the map. Data comes from NASA Solar System Treks, the PDS Analyst’s Notebook and JPL Photojournal. Narration uses the browser’s built-in text-to-speech. We tested layout with Playwright at six screen sizes, from a 1918-pixel desktop to a 390-pixel phone, and deployed on Vercel.

AI disclosure: we used Antigravity for coding and source checking, and Claude for early research, structuring the story and reviewing the design. The team directed the project, and we checked the facts against NASA’s own pages.
